questions.question: On a two-socket server, a thread on socket 0 reads memory physically attached to socket 1 and sees noticeably higher latency than reads from its own socket's DIMMs. What architecture name describes this asymmetry?
questions.explanation: NUMA (non-uniform memory access) systems share one address space, but access time depends on whether the DRAM is local or attached to another socket via an interconnect.

questions.question: Two threads update two completely different int counters, yet performance collapses because the counters happen to sit in the same 64-byte cache line, which ping-pongs between the cores' caches. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: Coherence works at line granularity, so independent variables sharing one line invalidate each other on every write — false sharing. Padding or per-thread copies fix it.

questions.question: In a fork/join runtime, one worker's deque empties while a busy neighbor's still holds forty queued tasks; the idle worker pops one from the busy deque's tail. What scheduling strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Work stealing keeps per-worker deques and lets idle workers pull tasks from busy ones, achieving load balance without a central queue bottleneck.

questions.question: Core 0 writes a data value then sets a 'ready' flag, but on a weak memory model Core 1 observes the flag before the data. The programmer inserts an instruction that forbids the reordering. What is it?
questions.explanation: A memory fence (barrier) orders memory operations so writes before it are visible before writes after it, preventing the flag-before-data reordering described.

questions.question: A theorist analyzes a sorting algorithm assuming N processors with lockstep, unit-cost access to one shared memory — deliberately ignoring communication cost to get a clean complexity bound. Which model is she using?
questions.explanation: PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) is the parallel analog of the RAM model: idealized synchronous shared-memory processors, with variants (EREW/CREW/CRCW) for concurrent access.

questions.question: A team benchmarks a fixed 1 TB simulation on 8, then 16, then 32 nodes, hoping the runtime halves each time — the problem itself never grows. Which scaling regime are they measuring?
questions.explanation: Strong scaling holds total problem size constant and measures speedup as processors grow; weak scaling instead holds work-per-processor constant and grows the problem.

questions.question: In a tagged-token machine there is no program counter at all: an add fires the instant both of its operand tokens arrive, and independent operations execute whenever their data is ready. What architecture model is this?
questions.explanation: Dataflow machines schedule by operand availability — an instruction's firing rule is 'all inputs present' — exposing maximal parallelism without sequential fetch.

questions.question: A solver splits its work into 200,000 tasks of about 100 microseconds each, and synchronization overhead now exceeds the actual computation. What granularity of parallelism is this?
questions.explanation: Fine-grained parallelism chops work into many tiny tasks with frequent synchronization; when task time approaches overhead, efficiency collapses — exactly the symptom shown.

questions.question: A render farm hands each node an entire film frame — several minutes of self-contained work — and exchanges only a single result message when the frame is done. What granularity of parallelism is this?
questions.explanation: Coarse-grained parallelism uses large, mostly independent tasks with rare communication, so overhead is negligible — the opposite of fine-grained division.

questions.question: Threads execute their critical sections speculatively without taking locks; hardware tracks their read/write sets and, on detecting a conflicting access from another thread, rolls one of them back to retry. What mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Transactional memory (hardware TM like Intel TSX, or software STM) makes a region of memory operations appear atomic: commit if no conflict, else abort and retry.

questions.question: A program is 95% parallelizable. Using 32 processors, what is the maximum speedup according to Amdahl's Law? (Round to two decimals.)
questions.explanation: Speedup = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/32) = 1 / 0.0796875 = 12.55, far below the linear speedup of 32 because of the serial fraction.

questions.question: Fault-tolerant flight-control computers running the same input data through multiple different algorithms fit which Flynn's taxonomy category?
questions.explanation: Multiple instruction streams operating on a single data stream is MISD, a rare class used in redundant fault-tolerant systems.

questions.question: Core A holds a cache line in the Modified state; Core B then reads the same address, forcing A's line to write back and both copies to end Shared. Under which four-state snooping protocol do these transitions occur?
questions.explanation: The M->S demotion on a snooped read, along with the Exclusive and Invalid states, is classic MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid govern each line's coherence lifecycle.

questions.question: A parallel program achieves a speedup of 9.1 on 10 processors. What is its parallel efficiency?
questions.explanation: Parallel efficiency = speedup / number of processors = 9.1 / 10 = 0.91 or 91%.

questions.question: What is the diameter (maximum distance between any two nodes) of a 16-node hypercube interconnect network?
questions.explanation: A hypercube with 2^n nodes has diameter n; since 16 = 2^4, the longest shortest path between nodes is 4 hops.

questions.question: Using Amdahl's law, what speedup does a program that is 90% parallelizable achieve on 8 processors?
A program is 95% parallelizable. According to Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speedup attainable even with infinitely many processors?
A parallel application achieves a speedup of 6 on 8 processors. What is its parallel efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = speedup / processors = 6 / 8 = 0.75 = 75%.

questions.question: A GPU kernel applies the same instruction simultaneously to thousands of independent pixels. Under Flynn's taxonomy, which class does this represent?
questions.explanation: One instruction stream operating on many data elements is SIMD; GPUs implement it as SIMT, the SIMD-style subdivision.

questions.question: A program runs for 100 seconds serially; 80% is perfectly parallelizable across 4 processors. What is the new total execution time?
questions.explanation: Serial part = 20 s; parallel part = 80/4 = 20 s; total = 20 + 20 = 40 s (speedup 2.5x).
